name: PT Victoria Care Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Victoria Care Indonesia — a premium rating for a business that just lost its margin
frontmatter.summary: Victoria Care keeps growing sales but not profit: marketing and input costs have cut the EBIT margin roughly in half, and the shares still trade on a premium multiple for a business whose return on equity now sits at its cost of capital. We initiate at SELL — the price needs a margin recovery the evidence does not support.
thesis: Sales momentum is real — revenue grew through the first nine months of 2026 — but profit fell because selling and marketing spend rose faster than sales, and that is the number that matters.

Gross margin has fallen to the low fifties as input costs rose, and trade discounts and returns already absorb about a quarter of gross sales, so there is little room to buy volume back without giving away margin.

The shares are priced at 36.8x our FY2027E earnings and 5.0x the last reported book for a return on equity near the cost of equity; our DCF, the method that fits a branded consumer, is worth Rp312 a share.
The controlling family sold a block at a discount to market in October 2026 and still owns the overwhelming majority of the company, so the float is thin and the overhang is live.

catalysts.event: FY2026 results — whether the fourth quarter confirms the Q3 margin recovery or the year lands at the low end of our profit forecast
Fourth-quarter trading and any year-end trade-spend true-up
Dividend for FY2026 — payout against the stated cap, and whether the controller takes cash
Premium relaunch and export push into Japan and other Asian markets

blocks.text: **SELL, target Rp402 (-50.2% total return from Rp820).** The market is paying a franchise multiple for a company whose profitability has just reset lower. Victoria Care's revenue grew in the first nine months of 2026, but net profit fell by more than a quarter against the prior year, to 87.7bn from 119.1bn [S5]. The cause is visible in the nine-month accounts: selling and marketing expense reached 342.5bn and general and administrative expense 132.0bn, a combined 42.3% of revenue, while gross profit barely moved and operating expense took the rest [S5]. A business that earned an EBIT margin of 16.7% in FY2024 now earns 10.0% [S3]. The history behind that comparison has been rebuilt from the audited accounts since the previous version: FY2025A revenue 1,410.7bn, operating expense 603.2bn, profit from operations 184.9bn, D&A 30.4bn and EBITDA 215.3bn at an EBITDA margin of 15.3%, with FY2024A on the same basis [S3]. The target is unchanged by that correction, and it should be: the DCF is built bottom-up from revenue and cost ratios, so the restated base moves the compression narrative, not the forecast. EBITDA still falls from 215.3bn to 188.2bn in FY2026E.

Our target is built on a DCF that anchors the company to a return on equity at its cost of capital. That is not a bearish assumption — it is what the last two years of returns say. Return on equity was 12.9% in FY2025 and we forecast 10.2% for FY2026E against a cost of equity of 11.1% [S3]. When a company earns its cost of capital, incremental growth adds little value, and the price should sit near book value plus a modest premium for the brand portfolio. The shares trade at 5.0x the last reported book value — 4.4x our FY2027E book — and 36.8x our FY2027E earnings.

The variant view is not that Victoria Care is a bad company. It owns two of the better-known mass beauty brands in Indonesia — Herborist and Miranda among others — and its personal-care and hair-care franchises together turned over a net-revenue base bigger than the consolidated total — 763.7bn of personal care and 677.3bn of hair care, before eliminations — out of 1,834.2bn of gross sales before trade discounts [S3]. The variant view is that the economics of defending those brands have changed. The annual report itself says new brands with aggressive promotion created significant competitive pressure on market share and pricing, and that the company had to spend more on marketing than the year before to hold awareness [S2]. That is a cost line that does not come back quickly.

Three things move the value. First, the gross-margin and marketing ratio: every point of margin held is worth materially more than a point of growth at this multiple. Second, whether the premium relaunch and export push promised for 2027 produce sales at a better mix, or merely more marketing [S6]. Third, the ownership overhang: the controller sold a block at a discount to market in October 2026 and still holds the large majority of the shares [S7], which caps how far a re-rating can run.

The price we are measuring that return from is itself a thin-float print. The shares had nearly doubled in the two months before the October block, the block cleared at a price about two-fifths below the prior close, and the stock now trades at Rp820, roughly a third below the pre-block level and inside a twelve-month range of Rp492 to Rp1,295, with only about a fifth of the shares in public hands and a register of roughly two thousand investors [S7]. A multiple near forty times trailing earnings struck on that float is not a clean franchise multiple — it may be a momentum residue left by a small free float, and the stock has already given back a large part of the run that produced it. We test that possibility rather than assume it: the DCF carries 70% of the target precisely because it does not rely on the market's multiple, and the scenario section states what happens if the multiple normalises.

Our target is a blend. The DCF is worth Rp312; a PE cross-check is worth Rp586 because it capitalises last year's earnings at the stock's own historical multiple, which we think is the number that is wrong; the dividend-yield cross-check is worth Rp357 because it embeds neither a recovery nor a de-rating. Weighted, the fundamental value is Rp360, and rolling it forward one year at the cost of equity gives a twelve-month target of Rp402. Because the PE leg is the odd one out — it is the only leg that assumes the market's multiple survives — we say plainly what the target would be without it: the dividend leg is 14.3% above the DCF, so the two weighted together come close to the DCF's Rp312, and the target would be correspondingly lower. It stays in the blend at a cross-check weight so the reader can see the price the market is paying, not because we believe it.

Victoria Care listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in 2020. Indonesian personal care is a
structurally attractive market: a young population, rising hygiene and skincare penetration, and a
large mass-market tier where local brands compete with Unilever, L'Oréal and a wave of Korean-inspired
labels. The usual local advantage is distribution density across Java and the outer islands, and the
usual vulnerability is that brand loyalty in mass cosmetics is thin and promotional.

Victoria Care manufactures and sells cosmetics and toiletries in Indonesia, with a small export business. It reports three segments: personal care and antiseptic (skincare creams and lotions, make-up, body scrubs, soaps, perfume, deodorant, and antiseptic liquids, gels and soaps); hair care (shampoo, hair masks, colouring, curling and straightening products); and others, a small line of coffee, souvenirs and snacks plus wholesale trading of pharmaceutical and laboratory equipment [S2]. The portfolio spans mass and masstige brands — Miranda, Herborist, Victoria, Nuface, Creative Beauty Dazzle Professional, Secret Clean, Sixsence and Bath & Buff — with Herborist positioned on natural and heritage ingredients [S0, S2].

The segment mix is unusually balanced for a company of this size. In FY2025 personal care and antiseptic generated 763.7bn of net segment revenue and hair care 677.3bn, with the others line negligible; both are net of trade discounts, and together they exceed consolidated net revenue before eliminations [S3]. Both segments carry gross margins in the mid-fifties at the segment-result line, so the profit problem is not mix between the two; it is what happens below the gross-profit line [S3]. Hair care is the more promotion-intensive of the two, and it is the segment where the annual report flags the most competitive pressure.

The revenue build has an unusual feature that matters for anyone modelling margins off the top line. Gross sales in FY2025 were 1,834.2bn, but net revenue was 1,410.7bn [S3]. The difference — roughly a quarter of gross sales — is trade discounts, rebates and returns. That is the price of shelf space in Indonesian modern trade and general trade, and it means headline price increases do not translate one-for-one into net revenue. It also means the company has a ready lever to buy volume, at a cost, when competition intensifies. Management has used it: gross sales fell slightly in FY2025 while net revenue rose, so the net-to-gross ratio improved a little, but the absolute trade spend remains large [S3].

Geographically the business is domestic. Of FY2025 gross sales, Java accounted for the large majority, the outer islands for most of the rest, and exports for 4.0bn — a rounding error [S3]. The export line is nonetheless the centrepiece of the 2027 plan: management told the press after the October 2026 shareholder meeting that it is preparing an expansion into the premium segment and international markets, with Japan among the targets, and expects sales growth to reach double digits by the end of 2026 [S6]. The company has exported to Japan, China, Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines, Brunei and Hong Kong for years without the line ever becoming material, which is why we treat the export story as optionality rather than as a forecast driver [S0].

Manufacturing is concentrated at the company's Semarang plant, which has been the operating base since 2007, with product development handled by an in-house research and innovation team [S2]. Management names production-capacity readiness as a focus area for the coming year, alongside a portfolio shift toward higher-profitability products [S2]. The company employed 2,543.0 people at the last count [S0].

The competitive position is challenger, not leader. Victoria Care is a sub-scale player against the multinationals in mass personal care and against a long tail of local brands in hair colour and skincare; the annual report does not disclose market share, and none of the sources we hold give a reliable number [S2]. Its advantages are brand recognition in specific categories — Herborist in natural personal care and Miranda in hair colour both won Top Brand awards in 2025 — and a manufacturing base with halal certification, which won the company a national halal cosmetics award [S2]. Its disadvantage is that those awards sit in categories where the entry cost for a new brand is low and the promotional arms race is expensive.

The group's controlling shareholder is PT Sukses Sejati Sejahtera, the vehicle associated with Anne
Vabila Salim, and
the founding Widjaja family remains in management. In October 2026 the company appointed Rahayu
Saraswati Dhirakanya Djojohadikusumo — a niece of President Prabowo and a sitting legislator — as
deputy president commissioner. Press coverage frames the company as politically affiliated; we treat
that as a governance fact to be monitored rather than as an operating input.

The Indonesian cosmetics and personal-care market is large, growing, and brutally competitive at the mass end. The company's own account of 2025 is a good summary of the industry's condition: global economic uncertainty, geopolitical volatility and changes in international trade policy affected the beauty and personal-care sector; domestic consumer purchasing power was under pressure; and consumer trends shifted quickly [S2]. Against that, public awareness of health, hygiene and sustainability supported demand for natural-based personal care products, which is the company's core strength, and supported domestic market growth [S2]. The same passage names the two cost pressures that hit the P&L in 2026: exchange-rate fluctuations and rising global raw-material prices [S2].

For our model, the relevant commodity deck is agricultural, not because Victoria Care sells commodities but because palm-derived surfactants, fatty alcohols and glycerin are part of its raw material basket. The house deck has CPO at US$1,007/t in FY2025 rising to US$1,240/t in FY2027E before easing to US$1,150/t in the long run. On our estimate only about a tenth of cost of goods sold is palm-linked, and only half of a cost move is recovered in price within the year, so the CPO path is a second-order driver of gross margin — worth watching, not worth building the thesis on. The bigger input story in 2026 was the mix of all raw materials plus packaging, which the auditor describes as the substance of inventory [S3].

Regulation matters in two places. Cosmetics require BPOM notification and, since the halal certification regime, halal assurance for products sold in Indonesia; Victoria Care's halal certification is an asset here rather than a compliance burden, and the company won the national halal cosmetics industry award in 2025 [S2]. The second regulatory channel is trade policy: the annual report explicitly cites changes in international trade policy as a sector influence, which for a producer of imported raw materials and packaging means the rupiah and any tariff change flow straight into cost of goods sold [S2].

The competitive landscape is the heart of the investment case. The annual report is unusually direct: the arrival of various new brands with aggressive promotional strategies created significant competitive pressure on market share and pricing, and in response the board adjusted strategy toward strengthening the body-care and hair-care portfolio, accelerating new product launches and continuous innovation [S2]. Later in the same report it says competition in cosmetics is intense enough that the company must spend more on marketing than the previous year simply to keep awareness and defend share, which is why the year deviated from its own target [S2]. That is the mechanism behind the profit decline: the company is paying more to stand still.

On Porter's five forces, the picture is unfavourable at the mass end and better in the niches the company is trying to occupy. Supplier power is moderate — commodity chemicals and packaging are available from many suppliers, but imported inputs expose the company to the rupiah. Buyer power is high: modern trade and the large distributors control shelf access, which is exactly what the trade discount line represents, and consumers switch on price and promotion. The threat of new entrants is high, because contract manufacturing and e-commerce lower the cost of launching a cosmetics brand. Substitutes are plentiful and cheap. Rivalry is intense and rising, per the company's own disclosure [S2]. The one force that works in Victoria Care's favour is the difficulty of replicating distribution reach across the outer islands and of building a brand that general trade will stock.

The moat, in other words, is brand plus distribution density, and the evidence that it is widening is weak. A widening moat would show up as stable or falling marketing intensity with stable share. What the accounts show is the opposite: operating expense was 603.2bn in FY2025 on 1,410.7bn of revenue [S3], and in the first nine months of 2026 selling and marketing alone reached 342.5bn and general and administrative expense 132.0bn on 1,120.0bn of revenue [S5]. That is the single most important number in this report, and it is why we do not give the company the benefit of a no-fade DCF.

Demand is also exposed to the macro deck. Indonesian CPI is forecast at 3.3% in FY2027E and the policy rate at 5.8%; the rupiah is forecast at Rp18,350/USD to the dollar. Mass personal care is a defensive category in a downturn, but the trade-down is real: consumers switch to cheaper brands rather than stop buying, which is precisely the pressure the annual report describes [S2]. A cheaper rupiah raises the cost of imported raw materials and packaging, and the company has limited pricing power to offset it in the mass tier.

The standard Indonesian consumer story — a rising middle class, per-capita spending S-curves, and
distribution as the moat — has been true for decades and has nonetheless produced a poor base rate for
premium-multiple personal-care stocks on the IDX over the past ten years. The names that de-rated did
so because marketing intensity rose and margins fell, not because the market shrank. We apply that
base rate here: a mid-single-digit growth category does not support a multiple in the forties unless
the margin is expanding.

**Revenue.** Victoria Care grew revenue from 1,045.7bn in FY2022A to 1,404.1bn in FY2024A, then stalled at 1,410.7bn in FY2025A, a growth rate of 0.5% [S3]. The first half of 2026 broke the stall: revenue reached 745.3bn, up by roughly a tenth on the prior-year half in the comparative column of the same statement [S4], and the nine months reached 1,120.0bn, up about a tenth on the prior-year period, on the run-rate behind the double-digit growth management is guiding to for the full year [S5, S6]. We carry that nine-month rate into FY2026E rather than assuming a fourth-quarter stall: 1,548.9bn, growth of 9.8%, then fade to 7.0% in FY2027E and about five per cent by FY2030E. The fade is deliberate: the AR describes a category where new entrants can buy share with promotion, and the company's own plan relies on a premium relaunch and exports that have never been material [S2, S6].

**Gross margin.** Gross margin was 55.9% in FY2025A, essentially unchanged from FY2024A [S3]. Through nine months of 2026 the reported figures give 589.4bn of gross profit on 1,120.0bn of revenue, and the third quarter alone was a shade below the first half rather than above it, so the cost spike had not unwound by September [S4, S5]. We therefore set FY2026E at 52.3% — essentially the reported nine-month margin, with the CPO cost link taking a few tenths of a point — and build only to 53.0% by FY2028E on premium mix, leaving the FY2025 and FY2024 levels well above anything we forecast [S0, S2]. The CPO link is the only input adjustment in the model: with the deck's CPO path rising into FY2027E and only partial pass-through, it shaves those tenths from gross margin in the near years.

**Costs and margins.** The profit decline is an operating-expense story. Operating expense rose to 603.2bn in FY2025A from 552.7bn in FY2024A, and in the nine months of 2026 selling and marketing reached 342.5bn and G&A 132.0bn — together a 42.3% operating-expense ratio, below the FY2025 level even as revenue grew [S3, S5]. The FY2025 operating-expense line is the segment note's unallocated operating expense, which by construction equals gross profit less the filed profit from operations; it is a little over two billion rupiah above the statement's selling-and-marketing line of 429 IDR bnbn plus G&A of 172 IDR bnbn, because it carries the net other operating charge [S3]. That is the line the model now uses, restated from the filing: the data pack had it seven billion rupiah too low and EBIT the same amount too high, so gross profit less operating expense now ties to the filed profit from operations in both years [S3]. EBIT fell from 234.9bn in FY2024A to 184.9bn in FY2025A and we forecast 154.9bn for FY2026E, an EBIT margin of 10.0% against 13.1% [S3].

The quarterly path inside the nine months deserves care, because it points two ways. Revenue in the third quarter was only the nine-month total less the first half, and on that arithmetic the third quarter's selling and marketing fell to about a quarter of its sales from about a third in the first half, with G&A near a tenth, which lifts its EBIT margin well above the nine-month average and about three points above our FY2027E forecast [S4, S5]. That is the red team's strongest point and it cuts both ways: if the third-quarter ratio is genuine, our base is too conservative; if it is under-spend, costs must catch up and the base is too high. We do not extrapolate it for two reasons. No disclosure explains the drop in selling and marketing — there is no release, no reclassification note and no commentary in the results statement we hold — and the summer quarter is seasonally lighter for promotional spend in Indonesian personal care. So we take the nine-month actual as FY2026E, ease to 39.5% by FY2030E — halfway toward the third-quarter exit rate — and give the full normalisation to the bull case rather than the base. The annual report gives the reason the ratio should not simply collapse: competition forced higher marketing spend to defend share [S2]. The scenario section states what happens to the value if the third-quarter ratio instead proves durable, and what happens if it was under-spend that catches up.

**D&A and the data pack.** The data pack prints FY2025 D&A far below the filing — the difference is the right-of-use depreciation, which the pack omits. The financial statements show total depreciation and amortisation of 30.4bn [S3]. We have restated FY2025 and FY2024 D&A from the filing, and on the filed profit from operations the historical EBITDA is 215.3bn, an EBITDA margin of 15.3%. The earlier draft added the restated D&A to a data-pack EBIT that was itself seven billion rupiah too high, which double-counted the correction and put historical EBITDA about the same amount above the filing; both inputs are now restated, so the base is the filing's own number [S3]. The restatement matters because it makes the FY2026 margin compression explicit rather than hidden: EBITDA falls to 188.2bn in FY2026E despite higher revenue — a fall of roughly an eighth, still a material reset, and the basis of the SELL.

**Cash flow and working capital.** Operating working capital is the swing factor in the cash flow, and the June 2026 balance sheet changes the picture we carried at initiation. At the FY2025 close it was 554.5bn, about two-fifths of revenue, with inventory at 337.6bn and the auditor naming inventory obsolescence as its key audit matter [S3]. But at 30 June 2026 trade receivables plus inventory less trade payables came to less than the December figure even though first-half sales grew by about a tenth: inventory fell against the December level even as sales rose, lifting inventory turns, so the stock was converted into cash rather than sitting in the warehouse [S4]. We therefore model the operating working-capital ratio on the June evidence — 36.8% of revenue, easing to 35.0% — not the FY2025 closing level ratio, because the release shows the marginal rupiah of sales does not consume working capital at the level ratio. Free cash flow was 150.8bn in FY2025A when revenue was flat; we forecast 90.6bn in FY2026E and 111.9bn in FY2027E. Capex is modest — 24.6bn in FY2025A, of which 16.9 IDR bnbn was fixed assets and advances and 7.7 IDR bnbn cash paid for right-of-use assets, both lines in the investing section of the cash-flow statement, after a plant-expansion year in FY2024A [S3] — and we model 3.0% of revenue, slightly above D&A, to fund premium-line capacity. The data pack's capex figure is the sum of those two lines, so the model line and the cash-flow statement reconcile to the rupiah. The nine-month release in our record is a results summary and does not include a cash-flow statement, so the June balance sheet is the best evidence we hold for the release; the first thing to check in the full-year accounts is whether operating cash flow confirms it.

**Balance sheet and capital allocation.** Leverage is not the issue: 72.1bn of cash against 85.1bn of debt in our FY2026E forecast, with net debt to EBITDA of 0.1 [S0]. The valuation bridge subtracts reported net debt, not our forecast, and that figure comes from the data pack's 30 September 2026 balance sheet: it is small enough not to decide the value either way, but it is unverified against a filing [S0]. The company's investor site carries the March and June 2026 statements and the audited FY2025 accounts, not the September quarter, so the last filed balance sheet is 30 June 2026, where net debt is roughly three times as large [S4]. Pack data for the third quarter show gross cash and gross debt each rising by more than a hundred billion rupiah while net debt fell by about thirty-six billion; a gross-up of borrowings held as deposits would produce that, and the retained third-quarter profit would produce the net move on its own [S0]. We keep the pack's net debt in the bridge, disclose that it is unverified, and quantify the alternative: on the June filing the DCF is about five rupiah a share lower, roughly one and a third per cent of the target, with no change to the rating [S4]. The first thing to check when the September accounts are filed is that cash-and-debt split; it is a bridge question, not a driver of the call. Capital allocation is simple: maintenance capex, a dividend at the policy cap, and the rest retained. The stated policy caps cash dividends at 40 per cent of net profit [S2]; FY2025 paid Rp8 per share — an interim and a final — of which the final is confirmed in cash by the first-half 2026 equity statement, and the total comes close to the cap [S4, S8]. The data pack reports only the final, so we restate the per-share figure from the company's own disclosure [S8]. We model a payout of 39.0%, the observed FY2025 rate rather than a cut we cannot source, because free cash flow after working capital covers it at the current margin.

**Earnings quality.** On the method card's tests, the earnings are cleaner than the margin trend would suggest, but not uniformly so. The accruals ratio was negative in FY2022, FY2023 and FY2025 and positive in FY2024, when profit ran about two and a half per cent of average assets ahead of operating cash flow; no year comes close to the ten-per-cent test, and FY2025 was the strongest cash year of the four, with free cash flow above net profit [S0]. The FY2024 exception is worth stating plainly rather than smoothing: the trend is improvement from a small positive accrual, not a series that was negative throughout, and the margin reset begins from that FY2024 peak. None of this is an earnings-quality red flag, which is the opposite of what a margin squeeze alone would suggest. The divergence flags were mixed at the FY2025 year-end — inventory had grown while cost of goods sold barely moved — but the June 2026 balance sheet reverses that: inventory fell while sales rose, so the year-end stock build has unwound and the flag no longer stands [S4]. What remains is receivables growing a little faster than revenue, consistent with extending terms in modern trade. We classify that as optics-class, not manipulation-class: the auditor's opinion is unqualified and there is no restatement and no going-concern language [S3]. Related-party sales to the controlling family's PT Natura Pesona Mandiri were 32.1bn in FY2025, a low-single-digit share of net sales — disclosed and small [S3]. The structure flags are ownership-related rather than accounting-related, and we deal with them in section six.

**Forecast summary.** By FY2027E we have revenue of 1,657.3bn, EBIT of 198.2bn (12.0%), net profit of 149.6bn and EPS of 22.3 [S0, S3, S4]. That is a recovery from the 2026 trough but still well below FY2024 profitability. Return on equity reaches 12.4% against a cost of equity of 11.1% — a business earning its cost of capital, not more.

**Why this method set.** Victoria Care is a branded consumer manufacturer with a visible cost structure, modest leverage and a dividend. The house method card for compounders and quality franchises puts a discounted cash flow first, with PE and dividend-yield cross-checks, and that is the right set here: the value depends on margins and reinvestment, not on a commodity price or a book of receivables. We weight the DCF at 70%, the PE cross-check at 15% and the dividend-yield cross-check at 15%. That is a deliberate departure from the industry default, which puts a third on the PE leg: here the PE leg capitalises LAST-ACTUAL net profit at the very multiple this report argues is wrong, so a third weight would let the rejected multiple set a third of the target. We halve it to a cross-check weight, move the freed weight to the dividend-yield leg, and say so in the justification file.
**Cost of capital.**

The build starts from a ten-year IDR risk-free rate of 7.4%, subtracts the default spread of 1.6%, and adds the relevered beta of 0.72 — from an unlevered 0.70 for debt at 0.03 of equity — multiplied by the SUM of the mature equity risk premium of 4.2% and the Indonesia country premium of 2.5%. The country premium sits inside the beta bracket, which is how the engine produces 11.1%: reading it as an additive term after the beta would overstate the cost of equity. On top we add the half-point premium for a single controller holding the large majority of the shares and a float that is still only about a fifth of the company after the October 2026 block [S7]. That gives a cost of equity of 11.1% and a WACC of 11.0% — the floor of the house eleven-to-thirteen per cent band for rupiah names, not its upper half, and we say so plainly so no reader mistakes the discount rate for a cautious one. The alternative reading, with the country premium added after the beta, would put the cost of equity near twelve per cent and cut the DCF by roughly a tenth; we tested it and the rating is unchanged. We keep the engine's build and the floor rather than pushing the discount rate up because the beta is the industry default and the premium already prices the ownership structure; the reader should note that the DCF is therefore flattered, and a cost of equity at the middle of the band would put the DCF lower still.
**Primary method.**

The DCF is worth Rp312 a share, an enterprise value of 2,108.2bn with the terminal value at 55.4% of the total. The terminal value share is high because the explicit forecast is a decade of modest growth; we hold terminal growth at 4.0%, below long-run Indonesian nominal GDP, and we let returns fade to the cost of capital by the end of the explicit period in line with the method card's fade discipline. There is no moat mechanism we can evidence as widening — marketing intensity is rising, not falling [S2] — so a no-fade DCF is not defensible here.
**Cross-checks and divergences.**

The P/E cross-check is worth Rp586, 87.8% above the DCF, and the dividend-yield cross-check is worth Rp357, 14.3% above it. The divergence is the point of this report. We must be precise about what the PE leg does, because the engine's PE method capitalises LAST-ACTUAL net profit — FY2025A, 136.7bn — at a blended multiple of 28.7; it does not apply that multiple to our FY2027E earnings. The leg is therefore a mark-to-market statement: it says what the shares would be worth if the market's own recent multiple were applied to the earnings this company actually delivered before the margin reset. That multiple is the market's belief that margins recover and the franchise deserves a premium. If the belief is right, the PE leg is the fair value; if the margin reset is structural, the multiple is what de-rates — and the leg is worth less than the last actual implies. Because the dividend-yield leg is only 14.3% above the DCF, those two legs are worth close to Rp312 between them: drop the PE leg and the blended value falls to about that level, with the twelve-month target correspondingly lower than Rp402. This is why the leg carries 15% and not a third: without it the blended value falls toward the DCF and dividend-yield cross-checks, which is the value we would defend if the multiple normalises. The method card's de-rating base rate for high-multiple Indonesian consumer names is poor, and the evidence in this company's own accounts — marketing up, EBIT margin down, return on equity at the cost of equity — points to de-rating rather than recovery. That is why the DCF carries the majority weight. The dividend-yield leg sits between the two because it capitalises a modest, policy-capped payout at a required yield and therefore embeds neither the recovery nor the de-rating.

**Multiple-survival test.** At today's price the shares trade at 36.8x our FY2027E earnings, 4.4x our FY2027E book and 23.3x EV/EBITDA, with a free-cash-flow yield of 2.0%. At that entry multiple the buyer's return depends almost entirely on the multiple holding while earnings grow: the cash yield alone does not earn the cost of capital, so the price requires a decade of growth far above the mid-single-digit rate we forecast — and the company's own plan is double-digit sales growth for one year, not a decade [S6]. Implied exit multiples above entry multiples are multiple expansion wearing a DCF costume; here the entry multiple is already above anything the fundamentals support.
**Sensitivity.**

The two inputs that carry most of the value are the operating-expense ratio and revenue growth, with gross margin third. A point of operating expense is worth more than a point of revenue growth at this cost structure, which is why the marketing line is the thing to monitor rather than the top line.

**What the price implies.** We could not bracket today's price with the reverse DCF: even at the top of the growth range the engine tests — several times our base-case revenue growth sustained for a decade — the DCF value does not reach Rp820. The price therefore implies either a margin recovery far beyond anything in the reported numbers or a multiple that never normalises. We are not prepared to underwrite either.

**Competition and marketing intensity — likelihood high, impact high.** The company's own disclosure says new brands with aggressive promotion created significant pressure on share and pricing, and that it must spend more to hold awareness [S2]. If that persists, our operating-expense assumption is too low, not too high, and the DCF falls further. This is the largest risk to our SELL being right in direction but wrong in magnitude.

**Gross-margin and input-cost risk — likelihood medium, impact medium.** Raw materials and packaging are the bulk of cost of goods sold [S3], and the rupiah and trade policy both feed into them [S2]. A weaker rupiah or a CPO spike would compress gross margin from the low fifties, and the company has limited pricing power in the mass tier. The house deck has CPO rising into FY2027E before easing, so the near-term direction is unhelpful.

**Governance and ownership — likelihood medium, impact high.** The controller holds the large majority of the shares, the free float is thin, and in October 2026 it sold a block at a discount to market [S7]. A controlling shareholder who is a willing seller at a discount sets a reference price below the market and caps re-rating. Related-party sales are small and disclosed, but the political appointment to the board adds a non-commercial dimension to decision-making [S2, S7].

**Liquidity and float — likelihood medium, impact medium.** Average daily value traded is IDR6.6bn, which is adequate for a small position but not for institutional size [S0]. A thin float amplifies moves in both directions, and the block-sale history means supply can appear at any time.

**Regulatory — likelihood low, impact medium.** Cosmetics notification and halal rules are a compliance cost rather than an existential risk, and the company is certified [S2]. The risk is that a regulatory change raises the cost of imported inputs or slows new product launches.

**Operational — likelihood low, impact medium.** Manufacturing is concentrated at one plant, and management flags production-capacity readiness as a focus area [S2]. A disruption would hit supply of the highest-margin lines first.

**Macro — likelihood medium, impact low to medium.** Mass personal care is defensive, but purchasing power pressure is explicitly cited as a 2025 headwind [S2]. Our macro deck has Indonesian CPI at 3.3% and the policy rate at 5.8% in FY2027E: a stable path, but not a consumer recovery.
**Scenarios.**

We run mirrored shocks on the three drivers that matter: revenue growth, gross margin and operating expense. In the bear case, growth is three points lower, gross margin a point and a half lower and the operating-expense ratio a point and a half higher — the first-half overspend becomes permanent — which leaves the value at Rp294. In the bull case, the premium relaunch works, growth is three points higher, gross margin a point and a half higher and operating expense a point and a half lower as launches annualise, giving Rp526. The base case is Rp393. The probability-weighted target is Rp402, and after rolling forward the fundamental value and allowing for dividends the twelve-month target is Rp402.

Note that even the bull case — a successful premium relaunch with better margins and marketing normalisation — is worth below today's price. That asymmetry is the strongest argument in the report: the market is not pricing the base case or the bull case as we can source them; it is pricing something better than both.

**The de-rating is not a scenario, it is the base case.** These scenarios shock margins and costs only; they do not shock the multiple, because the DCF does not contain one. That is deliberate. The SELL rests on a de-rating from 40.2x trailing earnings and 36.8x our FY2027E earnings, and the de-rating is quantified in the target itself: the DCF is worth Rp312 and carries 70% of the target, so a normalisation of the multiple is not a downside case added on top, it is the assumption the target is built on. The market has already begun that move — the stock trades at Rp820 against a peak of Rp1,295 within the past year — which is why the bear case is margin-only: the further compression our target assumes is another step of the same kind, not a new risk layered on a margin case. If we instead assumed the market's multiple survived, the answer would be the PE cross-check at Rp586, which we weight at 15% precisely because we do not believe it. A reader who wants the bear with a compressed exit multiple should note that the bear value of Rp294 already assumes a lower earnings base at the same cost of capital, and any de-rating on top would take the value below it.

The bull scenario of Rp526 sitting below the PE cross-check of Rp586 is not a contradiction. The bull improves margins and marketing inside a DCF that discounts at 11.0% and fades growth after the explicit period; the PE leg applies the market's own multiple to pre-reset earnings with no fade and no discount for the controller or the float. They answer different questions — what the business is worth if it recovers, and what the market would pay if it never re-rates — and the target weights the first heavily and the second lightly.

**Signposts that would change our view.** A full year of falling selling and marketing expense as a share of revenue with stable gross margin would tell us the competitive pressure is easing, and we would raise the base case. A credible, sized export contract — not a press ambition — would add a growth driver we have not modelled. Conversely, a further narrowing of the float or another discounted block sale would lower the price we think achievable even if the fundamentals stabilise.

**Ownership and control.** PT Sukses Sejati Sejahtera, the vehicle [S7] ties to Anne Vabila Salim, held 60.0 per cent of the shares at the FY2025 annual report date, alongside Beauty Brands International Pte Ltd at a quarter [S2]. Between then and October 2026 the controlling stake reached the mid-eighties; the stake arithmetic in the later disclosure implies the controller bought the foreign block, but we do not hold the acquisition disclosure itself, so we do not date or price that transaction and record the gap rather than fill it [S7]. On 9 October 2026 it sold 402.5m shares, about a sixteenth of the company, at Rp750 — a discount of 40 per cent to the prior close — leaving 79.0 per cent [S7]. Two things follow. First, the free float ROSE with that sale, from roughly fifteen per cent to about a fifth, so the ownership premium we charge in the cost of equity is for a register that is still thin rather than one that shrank; a fifth of the shares in public hands and 2,038 single investor identifications is thin by any standard, and it leaves the name's index treatment and liquidity hostage to a handful of holders [S7]. Second, no tender-offer document is in our record and we do not assert that one was required: control was already held at the annual-report date, so the block purchase changed the economic interest rather than creating a new control event, and a secondary block sale does not by itself trigger an offer. What we can say is that a controller who both bought and sold large blocks within weeks, the sale at a discount to market, is a governance fact investors should price — and we do, through the cost-of-equity premium [S7]. The data pack's float figure of 14.6% is dated after the block but is stale in substance: it reflects the register before the October 2026 transfers were processed, and the company's own block-sale disclosure puts the controller at 79.0% per cent after the sale [S0, S7].

**Board and management.** The founding family remains in the executive: Sumardi Widjaja is president director and Henny Soetanto is finance director [S0]. Billy Hartono Salim is president commissioner [S6, S8]. At the October 2026 extraordinary meeting shareholders appointed Rahayu Saraswati Dhirakanya Djojohadikusumo, a niece of the president, as deputy president commissioner [S6, S8]. She already held 2.4 per cent of the shares when appointed, which makes her a substantial shareholder as well as a commissioner — a concentration of interests we note rather than a finding of impropriety [S8]. The annual report sets out the board composition but we have not verified the independent-commissioner count against the regulatory minimum, so we make no claim about it here [S2]. We do not treat the political appointment as evidence of value destruction, but it is a reminder that board decisions are not purely commercial.

**Related parties.** Sales to PT Natura Pesona Mandiri, a related party, were 32.1bn in FY2025, or a low-single-digit share of net sales, up from a lower share in FY2024 [S3]. Interest was paid to a related party in FY2024 but not in FY2025 [S3]. The flows are small relative to revenue and disclosed, which is the best that can be said; they are not large enough to be the investment case either way.

**Audit and accounts.** The auditor issued an unqualified opinion on the FY2025 statements [S3]. The key audit matter is the allowance for inventory obsolescence, which is appropriate given that inventory is a quarter of total assets [S3]. There is no going-concern language and no restatement in the filings we hold, and we found no special-monitoring-board status or notation letter in the market data or filings we checked [S0, S3].

**Dividends.** The policy allows cash dividends of up to 40 per cent of net profit [S2]. FY2025 paid Rp8 per share in total — an interim and a final, the final paid in June 2026 — and the first-half 2026 statement of changes in equity confirms the final in cash; the total comes close to the policy cap [S4, S8]. The data pack carries only the final, so the per-share figure is restated from the company's own disclosure [S8]. The company has paid every year since listing [S0]. At the current price the trailing yield is 1.0%, which is not a reason to own the shares but is a reason the downside is not a zero.

**ESG.** The material issues are packaging waste — the company is a large user of plastic packaging in a market with weak collection infrastructure — and product safety and halal assurance, where the company's certification is a strength [S2]. Water and energy use in manufacturing are second-order. Governance is the weak pillar: concentrated control, a thin float, block trades at a discount and a related-party sales channel. On the social side, the company's brands target mass consumers and its distribution reaches the outer islands, which is a positive for consumer access rather than an ESG risk.

**Dated catalysts.** The FY2026 results in March 2027 are the key event: they will show whether the third-quarter margin recovery held through the fourth quarter or whether the year lands at the low end of our profit forecast [S3, S5]. The premium relaunch and export push promised for 2027 will be measurable from the first half of 2027 [S6]. The dividend for FY2026, declared around the middle of 2027, will show whether the controller is taking cash out or leaving it in the business [S2]. Any further block trade by the controller is a live catalyst given the October precedent [S7].

**What we watch between updates.** First, selling and marketing expense as a share of revenue — it is the single variable that decides whether the margin reset is cyclical or structural. Second, gross margin against the CPO deck: if CPO rises and gross margin holds, the pricing channel is working. Third, the net-to-gross ratio: if trade discounts widen again, the company is buying volume and the profit recovery is not real. Fourth, inventory days and the obsolescence allowance, given the auditor's focus. Fifth, the free float and any further controller sales. Sixth, any actual export revenue, as opposed to announced ambition [S2, S3, S5].

**What would make us wrong.** A durable recovery in EBIT margin toward the FY2024 level, achieved without a matching rise in marketing, would justify a multiple in the twenties and a much higher target. We would rather be shown that by two consecutive half-year reports than underwrite it now [S3, S5].

base.narrative: Sales grow high single digit on the 9M run-rate and the premium and export push, gross margin holds at the 52.6% 9M2026 level and inches up with premium mix, and marketing spend eases from the 9M ratio toward the third-quarter exit rate; profit recovers from the 2026 trough but never returns to the FY2024 margin.

bear.narrative: Competition forces marketing spend back to the 1H2026 peak while gross margin gives up the H1 cost spike and never recovers, so profit stagnates; the controller keeps selling blocks at a discount, capping any re-rating. The scenario is margin- and cost-only: the de-rating from the 41x multiple is already embedded in the DCF-weighted target, not assumed away here.

bull.narrative: Premium relaunch and the export push lift sales at a mid-teens rate from 2027, gross margin rebuilds toward the FY2024 level, and marketing intensity normalises as launches annualise, taking operating expense a point and a half below our base.

12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E carries the 9M2026 run-rate rather than a Q4 stall: 9M revenue was Rp1,120.7bn, +9.8% on the prior-year period (S5), management guides to double-digit growth for the full year (S6), and we hold that 9.8% into FY2026E with no assumption of a fourth-quarter slowdown. 1H2026 revenue grew 10.1% (S4), so the 9M rate is the through-year trend. The growth rate then fades to 7% in FY2027E and toward 5% by FY2030E because the AR itself describes intensifying competition from new brands with aggressive promotion (S2), so we do not extrapolate the double-digit plan beyond 2026.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the reported 9M2026 split, not on a recovery we cannot source: gross profit of Rp589.35bn on revenue of Rp1,120.7bn is a 52.6% gross margin (S5), and the third quarter was 51.8% after 1H's 53.0% (S4, S5), so the cost spike had not unwound by Q3. FY2026E is therefore 52.6%; the premium mix management targets lifts it to 54.0% by FY2030E, still below the 55.9% earned in FY2025 and the FY2024 level (S3), because trade discounts and returns already absorb a fifth of gross sales and competition is buying volume with promotion (S2, S3).

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: 10% of COGS. Palm-derived surfactants, fatty alcohols and glycerin are a minority of a personal-care bill of materials that the auditor describes as raw materials plus packaging (S3); the LK gives no CPO line, so this is a structural estimate for the palm-linked share only, not the whole raw-material basket.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: 50%. A branded portfolio can lift shelf prices but the AR shows marketing spend rising faster than sales when competition intensifies (S2), so only half of a CPO move is recovered within the year; the other half lands in gross margin.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Set to the 9M2026 actual: selling and marketing of Rp342.47bn plus G&A of Rp132.01bn on Rp1,120.7bn of revenue is 42.3% (S5), against FY2025's 42.6% (S3). The third quarter alone printed a much lower 36.6% (S&M 25.7% of sales, G&A 10.9%), but no disclosure explains that drop, so we do not extrapolate a single quarter; we ease from the 9M actual toward the Q3 exit rate over five years, crediting half of the observed improvement, because the AR says competitive pressure forced higher marketing spend to defend share (S2) and that spend does not disappear in one quarter.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated FY2025 D&A of Rp30.36bn is 2.15% of revenue (S3, including right-of-use depreciation); held at that ratio, consistent with maintenance capex.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Total capex was Rp24.6bn in FY2025 (1.7% of sales): Rp16.9bn of fixed assets and advances plus Rp7.7bn of cash paid for right-of-use assets, the two investing lines in the FY2025 cash-flow statement (S3), after a Rp96bn plant-expansion year in FY2024 which also reconciles as fixed assets plus right-of-use additions. With D&A at 2.2% of sales, 3.0% covers maintenance plus premium-line capacity, easing to 2.8% once the current investment cycle is complete.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Derived from the 30 June 2026 balance sheet, not the FY2025 closing ratio: trade receivables of Rp317.3bn (Rp302.7bn third party plus Rp14.6bn related party) and inventory of Rp307.9bn less trade payables of Rp80.6bn is operating working capital of Rp544.6bn, 36.8% of trailing revenue (S4). That is Rp21.1bn BELOW the Rp565.7bn at December 2025 even though sales grew 10.1%, because inventory days fell from about 87 to about 75 (S4), so the marginal intensity is far below the 39.3% level ratio we previously held. We start at the June level and ease to 35% as the release continues, rather than capitalising a one-off stock build into every future year.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 effective rate 23.0% (tax Rp40.9bn on PBT Rp177.7bn, S3); held at the statutory 23%.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Finance costs Rp7.78bn on opening debt of Rp85.1bn implies 9.1%; held at 8.75%, close to the FY2023-25 average (S3, S0).

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: House cap of 7% on the cash yield; FY2025 actual was 1.4% on a small average balance (S0), but the balance has grown and IDR deposit rates are near 5-6%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new term debt assumed; the company carries small gross debt and roughly balances it with cash, so the bridge uses the data pack's 30 September 2026 net debt of Rp15.6bn rather than calling the balance sheet net cash (S0). The last filed balance sheet, 30 June 2026, shows net debt about three times as large (S4); the September quarter is not yet filed, so the split is unverified and the June alternative would cut the DCF by about Rp5 per share (1.3% of target, no rating change).

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: No recurring other non-operating item is disclosed; FY2025 other income and expense net to a small loss inside operating profit (S3).

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: No minority interests on the balance sheet or in profit (S3).

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Policy caps cash dividends at 40% of the year's net profit [S2], and the FY2025 dividend shows the company running at that cap: interim Rp3 plus a Rp5 final paid in June 2026 is Rp53.66bn, 39.2% of FY2025 profit [S8]. The first-half 2026 statement of changes in equity confirms the Rp33.54bn final payment [S4]. We therefore hold 39%, the observed rate, rather than the lower figure the data pack's final-only dividend history implies; there is no sourced reason to assume the payout is cut.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue or buyback announced; 6,708m shares outstanding (S3).

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.0% nominal: mid-single-digit Indonesian personal-care market growth less the share erosion a 15-21% free float, sub-scale player faces against multinationals; at the house IDR long-run default.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E revenue of Rp1,519.3bn (growth 7.7%) implies Q4 2026 revenue of ~Rp398.6bn, only +2.0% on 2025 Q4, after 9M2026 revenue of Rp1,120.7bn (+9.8% YoY, S5) and management guidance of double-digit growth for the year (S6). Section 3 says the run-rate is 'consistent with the double-digit growth management is guiding to' and then forecasts below it. Revenue growth is one of the two drivers the report says carry the value (section 4 sensitivity).
challenges.answer: Revenue carries the 9M run-rate, not a Q4 stall: FY2026E revenue is now Rp1,548.9bn (+9.8%), i.e. the Rp1,120.0bn nine months annualised with no Q4 slowdown, consistent with S5's +9.8% and the double-digit guidance in S6. Growth fades to 7.0% in FY2027E because the AR's competition disclosure (S2) does not support extrapolating the plan beyond 2026.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E gross margin of 55.8% cannot be reconciled with the reported figures: 9M2026 gross profit was Rp589.35bn on revenue of Rp1,120.7bn, a 52.6% margin (S5), and 1H was 53.0% (F16). At 55.8% for the full year the implied Q4 gross margin is ~64.8% on a Q4 revenue of ~Rp398.6bn. The section 3 text says 'we hold FY2026E at 55.5%' and the QC justification says 'the recovery we model is only partial' when 55.8% is essentially a full recovery of the 55.9% FY2025 margin.
challenges.answer: FY2026E gross margin is 52.3% (52.6% input less the CPO link), the reported 9M margin, not 55.8%, and the text no longer claims a partial recovery to the FY2025 level. The bear gross margin is now 51.1%, below both the 9M 52.6% and the Q3 51.8%, so the bear is anchored below the last reported actual.

challenges.challenge: Opex is held at 45.5% of revenue in FY2026E and eased only to 43.5% by FY2030E, against a 9M2026 actual of 42.3% (S&M Rp342.47bn + G&A Rp132.01bn on Rp1,120.7bn, S5) and FY2025's 42.6%. The drift is anchored on the 1H spike (45.2%) that the company's own Q3 shows unwinding: Q3 S&M fell to Rp96.33bn, 25.7% of sales, and Q3 G&A to Rp41.10bn, 10.9%. Operating expense is the single largest value driver per section 4.
challenges.answer: Opex is set to the 9M2026 actual 42.3% (S&M Rp342.47bn + G&A Rp132.01bn on Rp1,120.0bn), below FY2025's 42.6%, easing to 39.5% by FY2030E, halfway to the Q3 exit rate. The five-year 45.5% drift is gone; there is no sourced reason to hold costs above the reported nine months.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 states the PE leg 'applies 28.7 ... to our FY2027E earnings', but the model (valuation.methods.pe.metric) capitalises FY2025A net profit of Rp136.74bn: 28.6686 x 136.739 / 6,708 = Rp584.4. The leg therefore values pre-reset earnings at a multiple that embeds the pre-reset franchise, at 30% of the target, while the same report calls that multiple 'the number that is wrong'. Dropping the leg as its own text implies would cut the target to ~Rp280.
challenges.answer: The text now states the metric the engine uses: LAST-ACTUAL FY2025A net profit of Rp136.74bn at 28.67x, not FY2027E earnings. We keep the leg at a 15% cross-check weight and quantify it: without the leg the DCF (Rp312) and dividend (Rp357) legs renormalise to about Rp320 fundamental and a target near Rp357, against Rp402 with the leg, so the leg adds roughly Rp45 of the target.

challenges.challenge: The COE of 11.13% is at the floor of the house 11-13% IDR band, not 'at the upper half' as section 4 claims. The stated build also does not reproduce the number: 7.45% - 1.62% + 0.72 x 4.23% + 2.46% + 0.5% = 11.8%; the engine reaches 11.13% only because the country premium is itself multiplied by the 0.72 beta (0.72 x (4.23% + 2.46%)).
challenges.answer: The report now states the band position and formula as the engine builds them: 11.1% COE and 11.0% WACC, the floor of the 11-13% band, with the country premium inside the beta bracket. The additive reading gives 11.8% COE and 11.7% WACC; we ran it and the DCF falls to Rp285 and the target to Rp382, still SELL, so the conclusion does not depend on the convention.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 justifies the +0.5pp COE premium with 'a free float that fell to around a fifth after the October 2026 block sale [S7]'. S7 shows the opposite: the controller sold 402.48m shares and its stake fell from 84.95% to 78.95%, so the float ROSE from ~15.1% to ~21.1%. Section 6 states the direction correctly, so the report contradicts itself in the paragraph that sets the discount rate.
challenges.answer: Direction corrected in the report and in coe_basis: the controller sold 402.48m shares, its stake fell from 84.95% to 78.95% and the float ROSE from about 15% to about 21% (S7). The half-point premium now rests on a 21% float still being thin, which is the defensible form of the argument.

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative says competition means 'profit stagnates and the multiple compresses', but the only bear shocks are revenue growth -3pp and gross margin -1.5pp; the PE leg keeps 28.67x and the dividend leg its yield, so the bear of Rp348 is only -11% from the base. The entire SELL thesis is a de-rating from a 41x multiple, and no scenario quantifies it.
challenges.answer: The de-rating is stated as the base case and quantified through the weights: DCF Rp312 carries 70% of the Rp402 target. The text adds the price history (Rp820 against a Rp1,295 peak) to show the market has already begun de-rating, and states that the bear (Rp294) is margin-only by construction at the same cost of capital.

challenges.challenge: The most recent quarter contradicts the base case and is not used: Q3 2026 EBIT was ~Rp54.9bn (9M Rp114.87bn less 1H Rp59.96bn, derived from S4/S5), a ~14.6% margin and roughly +13% YoY versus Q3 2025's ~Rp48.8bn, while the base case assumes FY2027E EBIT margin of 11.0%. The report cites Q3 only to justify a gross-margin assumption that Q3 actually contradicts (Q3 gross margin 51.8%, below 1H's 53.0%).
challenges.answer: Base FY2027E EBIT margin is 12.0%, not 11.0%: 1.8pp above the 9M 10.2% and 2.6pp below the Q3 14.6%, i.e. roughly two-fifths of the Q3 improvement is credited. Section 3 now states the Q3 margin and why we do not capitalise all of it: no disclosure explains the S&M fall and promotional spend is seasonal.

challenges.challenge: The 9M profit that anchors the thesis includes a quarter in which selling and marketing fell to Rp96.33bn, 25.7% of sales, from 33.0% in 1H. If that is under-spend, FY2027 costs must catch up and the base case's 11.0% EBIT margin is too high, not too low; if it is a reclassification, the gross-margin/opex split changes. The report cites S5 only for the profit number and never mentions the Q3 cost ratio.
challenges.answer: Section 3 discusses the Q3 cost ratio directly: S&M about a quarter of sales against about a third in 1H, G&A near a tenth, with no release or reclassification note in the results statement we hold. The base keeps the 9M ratio, the bear holds the 1H peak, and only the bull gives full normalisation, so the ambiguity is stated rather than hidden.

challenges.challenge: The model holds net working capital at 39.3% of revenue, which cuts FY2026E FCFF to Rp61.7bn from Rp156.3bn in FY2025 and is the single largest reason the DCF is Rp247. The June 2026 balance sheet shows inventory down to Rp307.9bn from Rp337.6bn at December 2025 (-8.8%) while 1H revenue rose 10.1%, i.e. inventory days fell from ~87 to ~75 (S4). The section 3 earnings-quality flag that 'inventory grew while cost of goods sold barely moved' is therefore stale and rejects the working-capital release.
challenges.answer: NWC is 36.8% of revenue from the 30 June 2026 balance sheet (receivables Rp317.3bn plus inventory Rp307.9bn less payables Rp80.6bn, on Rp544.6bn), not the 39.3% FY2025 level ratio, easing to 35%. FY2026E FCFF is Rp90.6bn. The 9M release in our record has no cash-flow statement, so the report says operating cash flow is the first thing to confirm in the full-year accounts.

challenges.challenge: The controller went from 59.95% at the annual-report date (F21) plus Beauty Brands International's ~25% (S2) to 84.95% by October 2026 (S7), i.e. it acquired the foreign block, then sold 6% at Rp750, a ~40% discount to the prior close. The report asserts the acquisition without a date, price or disclosure citation and never discusses tender-offer, free-float or index consequences, nor the fact that S7 puts the shareholder register at only ~2,038 SID.
challenges.answer: Rewrote the ownership section: we do not hold the Beauty Brands acquisition filing and now say so plainly instead of asserting an undated purchase. The block sale is sourced to S7 with price, size, discount and register (2,038 SID). We withdrew the unsourced 80%/tender-offer claim, since control was already held, and the unsourced free-float-minimum claim, and added F29: the new deputy president commissioner holds 2.4% of the shares (S8).

challenges.challenge: S7 states that the block was placed after the shares had risen almost 100% in two months, at Rp750 or ~40% below the prior close; the shares now trade at Rp820, ~34% below that pre-block level. The report never mentions the move, yet the -51.5% expected return is measured from that price and 'the market is paying a franchise multiple' is the central claim about it. A reader cannot tell whether 820 is a franchise multiple or a thin-float momentum residue.
challenges.answer: The rating rationale now carries the price history: shares nearly doubled into the October block, cleared at Rp750, now Rp820 inside a twelve-month range of Rp492-Rp1,295, with about a fifth free float. Section 5 tests whether the multiple is representative and concludes the target does not rely on it (DCF 70%), while flagging that a thin float can hold a multiple up.

EBITDA of Rp222.3bn for FY2025A is the pack EBIT of Rp191.9bn plus the restated D&A of Rp30.36bn, which double-counts the difference: the filing gives EBIT of about Rp184.9bn and EBITDA of Rp215.3bn. challenges.answer: Rebuilt FY2024A and FY2025A from the audited LK: operating expense now Rp603.20bn (the segment note unallocated line, which equals gross profit less filed operating profit, and is Rp600.94bn of S&M plus G&A plus the net other charge), EBIT Rp184.90bn (filed), D&A Rp30.36bn and EBITDA Rp215.27bn at a 15.3% margin; gross profit less opex now ties to filed EBIT in both years. On an equity value of about Rp2.7tn that is roughly 5% of the target and it is not sourced to the LK. QC FIX 5, unchanged.

missing_bull_case.note: The bull (Rp441) is worth less than the report's own static PE cross-check (Rp584) and gives no credit to the Q3 2026 exit economics: Q3 EBIT ~Rp54.9bn, ~14.6% margin (~+13% YoY), while the base assumes FY2027E EBIT margin of 11.0%. flags.message: dps FY2025A restated at 1.60x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The data pack carries only the Rp5 final dividend. The FY2025 dividend was Rp8 per share — a Rp3 interim plus the Rp5 final — Rp53.66bn in total, a 39.2% payout against the stated 40% cap [S8]. The first-half 2026 statement of changes in equity independently shows the Rp33.54bn cash dividend payment, confirming the final [S4]. The per-share history is therefore restated from the company's own disclosure rather than the pack's final-only series.

flags.message: expected return -50%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The -50% expected return comes from three sourced drivers, not from a valuation haircut. First, 9M2026 profit fell 26.4% to Rp87.72bn even as revenue rose 9.8%, because selling and marketing reached Rp342.47bn and G&A Rp132.01bn on Rp1,120.0bn of sales — a 42.3% operating-expense ratio and an EBIT margin near 10%, against roughly 14.6% in the third quarter alone [S5, S4]. Second, the gross margin earned through nine months is 52.6% (Rp589.35bn on Rp1,120.0bn) and the third quarter was lower still at 51.8%, so a full recovery to the FY2025 55.9% is not in the reported numbers [S5, S3]. Third, at Rp820 the shares are 40.2x FY2025A and 36.8x FY2027E earnings and 5.0x the last reported book value for a return on equity near the 11.1% cost of equity [S0, S4]; the reverse DCF cannot bracket that price even at the top of the growth range tested, so the price implies a margin recovery or a multiple that never normalises, neither of which the accounts support.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'pe': 0.3, 'div_yield': 0.1}
flags.justification: The house default 0.6/0.3/0.1 would leave the PE leg, which the engine computes on LAST-ACTUAL (FY2025A) net profit of Rp136.74bn at a 28.67x blended multiple, carrying 30% of the target while this report argues that multiple is exactly what de-rates [S0, S2]. We cut it to 15% and move the freed weight to the dividend-yield cross-check, so the target is driven by the DCF (70%) and the dividend yield (15%), and say so in section 4 rather than letting a rejected multiple set the value.
